title: "Scaling to 1000 GPUs"
subtitle: "At 1024 GPUs, communication overhead is the cost everyone talks about. Is it the dominant one?"
description: "Sweep from 8 to 1024 GPUs and discover which overhead actually dominates at scale. The answer is not what most engineers expect."
categories: ["fleet", "advanced"]
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import mlsysim  # installed via `pip install mlsysim` (see workflow)
from mlsysim import Models, Systems, Infrastructure
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel, ReliabilityModel, CheckpointModel, SustainabilityModel
from mlsysim.systems.reliability import Reliability
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet

Engine = mlsysim.Engine

_model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
_dgx = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
_ib = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
_dist_solver = DistributedModel()
_rel_solver = ReliabilityModel()
_ckpt_solver = CheckpointModel()

_params_b = _model.parameters.to("dimensionless").magnitude / 1e9
_gpus_per_node = _dgx.accelerators_per_node
_nvlink_gbs = _dgx.intra_node_bw.to("GB/s").magnitude
_ib_gbps = _ib.bandwidth.to("Gbps").magnitude

_gpu_mttf = Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours
_nic_mttf = Reliability.Nic.mttf_hours
_psu_mttf = Reliability.Psu.mttf_hours

_job_days = 30
_job_hours = _job_days * 24
_ckpt_time_s = 60.0

_gpu_counts = [8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]
_dist_results = {}
_rel_results = {}
for _n in _gpu_counts:
    _fl = Fleet(name=f"{_n}-GPU", node=_dgx, count=_n // _gpus_per_node, fabric=_ib)
    _dist_results[_n] = _dist_solver.solve(
        model=_model, fleet=_fl, batch_size=max(64, _n), precision="fp16", tp_size=_gpus_per_node, pp_size=1
    )
    _rel_results[_n] = _rel_solver.solve(
        fleet=_fl, job_duration_hours=_job_hours, checkpoint_time_s=_ckpt_time_s
    )

_comm_loss = {}
_ckpt_loss = {}
_ckpt_ratio = {}
for _n in [64, 256, 512, 1024]:
    _dr = _dist_results[_n]
    _rr = _rel_results[_n]
    _cl = (1.0 - _dr.scaling_efficiency) * _job_hours
    _cr = _ckpt_solver.solve(
        model=_model,
        hardware=_dgx.accelerator,
        optimizer="adam",
        checkpoint_interval_hours=_rr.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude,
    )
    _write_s = _cr.write_time_seconds.to("second").magnitude
    _int_h = _rr.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude
    _n_ckpts = _job_hours / _int_h if _int_h > 0 else 0.0
    _write_h = _n_ckpts * _write_s / 3600.0
    _rollback_h = _rr.expected_failures * (_int_h / 2.0)
    _tot_ckpt_h = _write_h + _rollback_h
    _comm_loss[_n] = _cl
    _ckpt_loss[_n] = _tot_ckpt_h
    _ckpt_ratio[_n] = _tot_ckpt_h / _cl if _cl > 0 else 0.0

_ckpt_1h = _ckpt_solver.solve(
    model=_model, hardware=_dgx.accelerator, optimizer="adam", checkpoint_interval_hours=1.0
)

_f256 = Fleet(name="256-GPU", node=_dgx, count=32, fabric=_ib)
_sust = SustainabilityModel()
_geo_ratio = (
    _sust.solve(fleet=_f256, duration_days=30, datacenter=Infrastructure.Grids.Poland).carbon_footprint_kg
    / _sust.solve(fleet=_f256, duration_days=30, datacenter=Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec).carbon_footprint_kg
)
```

## The Question

A team has `{python} _model.name` (`{python} f"{_params_b:.1f}B"` parameters) and a budget for `{python} _gpu_counts[-1]` `{python} _dgx.accelerator.name` GPUs. Communication overhead
(AllReduce, pipeline bubbles) will consume some of the scaling efficiency, as every
distributed-training engineer expects. How do communication overhead and cluster reliability
evolve as the fleet scales from `{python} _gpu_counts[0]` to `{python} _gpu_counts[-1]` GPUs over a `{python} _job_days`-day training run?

::: {.callout-note}
## Prerequisites
Complete [Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline](00_hello_roofline.qmd) and
[Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall](01_memory_wall.qmd). This tutorial assumes familiarity with
memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and the roofline model.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Objectives

- **Calculate** scaling efficiency across GPU counts from `{python} _gpu_counts[0]` to `{python} _gpu_counts[-1]`
- **Predict** cluster Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) using the reliability model
- **Compare** communication overhead vs. checkpoint overhead over a `{python} _job_days`-day training run
- **Explain** how checkpoint I/O and failure rollbacks scale with cluster size
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Background: Cluster Reliability and the Young-Daly Formula

At scale, hardware failures are not rare events; they are routine. In the MLSys Zoo, a single GPU has a
Mean Time To Failure (MTTF) of `{python} f"{_gpu_mttf:,.0f}"` hours, a NIC has an MTTF of `{python} f"{_nic_mttf:,.0f}"` hours, and a PSU has an MTTF of `{python} f"{_psu_mttf:,.0f}"` hours. A cluster of $N$ GPUs alone has a collective MTBF of
$\text{MTTF} / N$ (`{python} f"{_gpu_mttf / 512:.1f}"` hours at 512 GPUs). Including all node components (`{python} _gpus_per_node` GPUs, `{python} _dgx.nics_per_node` NICs, and `{python} _dgx.series_psus` non-redundant PSUs per `{python} _dgx.name` node) lowers the cluster MTBF to `{python} f"{_rel_results[512].fleet_mtbf.to('hour').magnitude:.1f}"` hours at 512 GPUs and `{python} f"{_rel_results[1024].fleet_mtbf.to('hour').magnitude:.1f}"` hours at 1024 GPUs.

To survive failures, training jobs checkpoint periodically: save the full model state
(weights + optimizer) to storage. The **Young-Daly formula** gives the optimal checkpoint
interval that minimizes total wasted time:

$$T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta \cdot M}$$

where $\delta$ is the time to write one checkpoint and $M$ is the cluster MTBF.
This assumes failures arrive as a Poisson process (exponentially distributed inter-arrival
times) and that on failure, work since the last checkpoint is lost (on average, half
the checkpoint interval). The cost of checkpointing is therefore not only the write time
but also this rollback time.
:::

## 1. Setup

```python
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine
```

## 2. Single-Node Baseline

The simplest case is `{python} _gpus_per_node` GPUs in a single `{python} _dgx.name` node (`{python} f"{_nvlink_gbs:.0f} GB/s"` intra-node NVLink per direction), with no cross-node data-parallel traffic. This configuration sets the ceiling for scaling efficiency.

```{python}
from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
solver = DistributedModel()

# Single DGX H100 node: 8 GPUs, NVLink interconnect
single_node = Fleet(
    name="Single Node",
    node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
    count=1,
    fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
)

baseline = solver.solve(
    model=model, fleet=single_node,
    batch_size=64, precision="fp16", tp_size=8, pp_size=1
)

info("Single-Node Baseline",
     GPUs=single_node.total_accelerators,
     Compute_latency=baseline.node_profile.latency.to('ms'),
     Communication=baseline.communication_latency.to('ms'),
     Scaling_efficiency=f"{baseline.scaling_efficiency:.1%}")
```

With `{python} _gpus_per_node` GPUs on a single node at batch size 64, compute takes `{python} f"{_dist_results[8].node_profile.latency.to('ms').magnitude:,.1f} ms"` and intra-node tensor-parallel AllReduce over NVLink takes `{python} f"{_dist_results[8].communication_latency.to('ms').magnitude:,.1f} ms"`, yielding a baseline scaling efficiency of `{python} f"{_dist_results[8].scaling_efficiency:.1%}"`.

This tutorial uses the three dimensions of **3D parallelism**:

- **TP (Tensor Parallelism)** = `{python} _gpus_per_node`: splits each layer's weight matrices across `{python} _gpus_per_node` GPUs within a node, communicating via NVLink (`{python} f"{_nvlink_gbs:.0f} GB/s"`)
- **PP (Pipeline Parallelism)** = 1: no pipeline stages (the model is not split across sequential stages), so no pipeline bubbles
- **DP (Data Parallelism)** = $N / `{python} _gpus_per_node`$: each node processes different data batches, synchronizing gradients via AllReduce over `{python} _ib.name` (`{python} f"{_ib_gbps:.0f} Gbps"`)

Setting PP=1 isolates the communication vs. reliability comparison cleanly. Real production
systems often use PP > 1 for models too large to fit on one node with TP alone, which
introduces pipeline bubble overhead (idle time proportional to $1/\text{PP}$ stages).

---

## 3. Scale Sweep: 8 to 1024 GPUs

The sweep below covers cluster sizes from `{python} _gpu_counts[0]` to `{python} _gpu_counts[-1]` GPUs. At each scale, it measures
communication overhead (intra-node TP AllReduce plus inter-node DP AllReduce) and scaling efficiency.

```{python}
gpu_counts = [8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]

rows = []
results = {}
for n_gpus in gpu_counts:
    n_nodes = n_gpus // 8
    fleet = Fleet(
        name=f"{n_gpus}-GPU Cluster",
        node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
        count=n_nodes,
        fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
    )
    # Use TP=8 within node, DP across nodes
    r = solver.solve(
        model=model, fleet=fleet,
        batch_size=max(64, n_gpus),
        precision="fp16", tp_size=8, pp_size=1
    )
    results[n_gpus] = r
    rows.append([
        n_gpus, n_nodes,
        f"{r.communication_latency.to('ms').magnitude:.1f}",
        f"{r.pipeline_bubble_latency.to('ms').magnitude:.1f}",
        f"{r.scaling_efficiency:.1%}"
    ])

table(["GPUs", "Nodes", "Comm (ms)", "Bubble (ms)", "Efficiency"], rows)
```

Once the global batch scales linearly with GPU count from 64 GPUs (`{python} f"{_dist_results[64].communication_latency.to('ms').magnitude:.1f} ms"` AllReduce, `{python} f"{_dist_results[64].scaling_efficiency:.1%}"` scaling efficiency) to 1024 GPUs (`{python} f"{_dist_results[1024].communication_latency.to('ms').magnitude:,.1f} ms"` AllReduce, `{python} f"{_dist_results[1024].scaling_efficiency:.1%}"` scaling efficiency), ring AllReduce bandwidth utilization stabilizes and scaling efficiency degrades gradually. This is **Amdahl's Law** in action: if the serial fraction (communication)
is $f$, the maximum speedup at $N$ GPUs is $1 / (f + (1-f)/N)$.

This communication analysis, however, assumes that every node stays healthy for
the entire `{python} _job_days`-day training run. Communication is not the whole story.

---

## 4. The Reliability Reveal

A separate question is how often a 64-GPU, 512-GPU, or 1024-GPU cluster experiences a
hardware failure. The `ReliabilityModel` computes cluster-level MTBF, expected failures, optimal checkpoint intervals, and steady-state goodput.

```{python}
from mlsysim.solvers import ReliabilityModel

rel_solver = ReliabilityModel()

rows = []
rel_results = {}
for n_gpus in gpu_counts:
    n_nodes = n_gpus // 8
    fleet = Fleet(
        name=f"{n_gpus}-GPU",
        node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
        count=n_nodes,
        fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
    )
    # 30-day training run, 60-second checkpoint write time
    r = rel_solver.solve(fleet=fleet, job_duration_hours=30*24, checkpoint_time_s=60.0)
    rel_results[n_gpus] = r
    mtbf_h = r.fleet_mtbf.to("hour").magnitude
    rows.append([
        n_gpus, n_nodes,
        f"{mtbf_h:.1f} h",
        f"{r.expected_failures:.1f}",
        f"{r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h",
        f"{r.goodput_ratio:.1%}"
    ])

table(["GPUs", "Nodes", "Cluster MTBF", "Failures/30d", "Optimal Ckpt", "Goodput"], rows)
```

At 64 GPUs, the cluster MTBF is `{python} f"{_rel_results[64].fleet_mtbf.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h"` (`{python} f"{_rel_results[64].expected_failures:.1f}"` expected failures over `{python} _job_days` days, `{python} f"{_rel_results[64].optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h"` optimal checkpoint interval, `{python} f"{_rel_results[64].goodput_ratio:.1%}"` steady-state goodput). At 512 GPUs, the cluster MTBF drops to `{python} f"{_rel_results[512].fleet_mtbf.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h"` (`{python} f"{_rel_results[512].expected_failures:.1f}"` failures over `{python} _job_days` days, `{python} f"{_rel_results[512].optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h"` optimal checkpoint interval, `{python} f"{_rel_results[512].goodput_ratio:.1%}"` goodput). At 1024 GPUs, MTBF reaches `{python} f"{_rel_results[1024].fleet_mtbf.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h"`, with `{python} f"{_rel_results[1024].expected_failures:.1f}"` expected failures in `{python} _job_days` days, an optimal checkpoint interval of `{python} f"{_rel_results[1024].optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h"`, and `{python} f"{_rel_results[1024].goodput_ratio:.1%}"` steady-state goodput. Every checkpoint pauses training, and every failure
rolls back to the last checkpoint, discarding all work in between.

---

## 5. The Hidden Cost: Communication vs. Checkpoints

The comparison below tracks how total time lost over a `{python} _job_days`-day (`{python} _job_hours`-hour) training run evolves across cluster sizes for both unoverlapped communication overhead and synchronous checkpoint plus rollback overhead.

```{python}
from mlsysim.solvers import CheckpointModel

ckpt_solver = CheckpointModel()
job_hours = 30 * 24  # 30 days

rows = []
for n_gpus in [64, 256, 512, 1024]:
    dist_r = results[n_gpus]
    rel_r = rel_results[n_gpus]

    # Communication overhead per step as fraction of step time
    comm_fraction = 1.0 - dist_r.scaling_efficiency
    comm_loss_hours = comm_fraction * job_hours

    # Checkpoint overhead: write time per checkpoint + rollback from failures
    ckpt_r = ckpt_solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerator,
        optimizer="adam", checkpoint_interval_hours=rel_r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude
    )
    ckpt_write_s = ckpt_r.write_time_seconds.to("second").magnitude
    ckpt_interval_h = rel_r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude

    # Number of checkpoints in 30 days
    n_checkpoints = job_hours / ckpt_interval_h if ckpt_interval_h > 0 else 0
    total_ckpt_write_h = n_checkpoints * ckpt_write_s / 3600

    # Rollback cost: each failure loses ~half the checkpoint interval on average
    avg_rollback_h = ckpt_interval_h / 2
    total_rollback_h = rel_r.expected_failures * avg_rollback_h

    total_ckpt_loss_h = total_ckpt_write_h + total_rollback_h
    ratio = total_ckpt_loss_h / comm_loss_hours if comm_loss_hours > 0 else 0

    rows.append([n_gpus, f"{comm_loss_hours:.1f}", f"{total_ckpt_loss_h:.1f}", f"{ratio:.2f}x"])

table(["GPUs", "Comm Loss (h)", "Ckpt Loss (h)", "Ckpt/Comm"], rows)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Insight

**While ring AllReduce overhead plateaus with cluster size, reliability overhead grows as $\sqrt{N}$.** Between 64 and 1024 GPUs, unoverlapped communication loss changes by only `{python} f"{(_comm_loss[1024] - _comm_loss[64]) / _comm_loss[64]:.1%}"` (from `{python} f"{_comm_loss[64]:.1f} h"` to `{python} f"{_comm_loss[1024]:.1f} h"` over `{python} _job_hours` hours), whereas synchronous checkpoint I/O and failure rollback losses grow `{python} f"{_ckpt_loss[1024] / _ckpt_loss[64]:.1f}×"` (from `{python} f"{_ckpt_loss[64]:.1f} h"` at 64 GPUs to `{python} f"{_ckpt_loss[1024]:.1f} h"` at 1024 GPUs, or `{python} f"{_ckpt_ratio[1024]:.0%}"` of the unoverlapped communication loss). When DP communication is overlapped with backward computation, checkpoint I/O and failure recovery become the primary scaling bottleneck.
:::

---

## 6. The Checkpoint Size Problem

Checkpoint overhead is costly because modern models produce large checkpoint files.
The cell below computes the checkpoint size for `{python} _model.name` with the Adam optimizer:

```{python}
ckpt_result = ckpt_solver.solve(
    model=model,
    hardware=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerator,
    optimizer="adam",
    checkpoint_interval_hours=1.0
)

info("Checkpoint Analysis",
     Model=model.name,
     Checkpoint_size=ckpt_result.checkpoint_size.to('GB'),
     Write_time=ckpt_result.write_time_seconds.to('second'),
     MFU_penalty_1h=f"{ckpt_result.mfu_penalty_pct:.2%}",
     Storage_bottleneck=ckpt_result.storage_bottleneck)
```

A single mixed-precision Adam checkpoint for `{python} _model.name` (`{python} f"{_params_b:.1f}B"` parameters at 14 bytes per parameter) is `{python} f"{_ckpt_1h.checkpoint_size.to('GB').magnitude:.1f} GB"` and requires `{python} f"{_ckpt_1h.write_time_seconds.to('second').magnitude:.1f} s"` of synchronous storage write time. At a 1-hour interval, checkpoint I/O alone imposes a `{python} f"{_ckpt_1h.mfu_penalty_pct:.2%}"` MFU penalty.
